query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coatings, a modulation period that yields semicoherent interfaces (specifically λ = 16 nm) results in localized stress concentrations that promote stress-induced interfacial amorphization. This amorphization lowers atomic-migration barriers and promotes an atomic-diffusion or interface-slip creep mechanism, thereby enhancing creep resistance compared to multilayers with coherent interfaces (λ = 8 nm) or grain boundary-dominated microstructures (λ = 32 and 80 nm) that deform predominantly via dislocation slip or climb.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, approximately 1 μm-thick FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings produced from Al0.2CrFeNi and Al targets.
generation.intervention: Vary the modulation period (individual layer thickness, λ) among 8, 16, 32, and 80 nm by RF magnetron sputtering. Follow deposition with room-temperature nanoindentation creep testing under specified load and dwell conditions.
generation.conditions: Deposition under ~5×10^-4 Pa base pressure, 100 sccm Ar, working pressure of 0.3 Pa, using 150 W on the HEA target and alternating 0/30 W on the Al target for a 1 h deposition. Nanoindentation performed with a 5 mN maximum load, loading rates from 1 to 0.01 mN/s, 100 s dwell, and 20 s unloading, maintaining indentation depths at about 1/10–1/7 of the coating thickness.
generation.structural_mediator: Interface coherency and the resulting local structural state; specifically, semicoherent FCC/BCC interfaces (λ = 16 nm) containing misfit dislocations lead to localized stress concentrations that can trigger interfacial amorphization.
generation.mechanism: Semicoherent interfaces, in contrast to coherent interfaces or grain boundaries, strongly block dislocation glide, leading to dislocation pileup and localized high stresses which in turn promote the formation of amorphous regions. These amorphous interfaces possess increased free volume, disorder, and high-energy boundaries that reduce the atomic-migration barrier, thereby enabling a controlled atomic diffusion or interface slip mechanism that redistributes stress and enhances creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under nanoindentation creep testing at room temperature, the λ = 16 nm (semicoherent) multilayer is expected to display superior creep resistance, evidenced by lower creep displacement and a lower effective creep stress exponent (n approaching values typical of diffusion/interface-slip creep around 1–2) compared to the λ = 8 nm (coherent) and λ = 32/80 nm (grain-boundary-dominated) samples, which should exhibit higher creep displacement and stress exponents (>3) indicative of dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.baseline: Coatings with λ = 8 nm (coherent interfaces) and λ = 32/80 nm (grain boundary-dominated) serve as the baseline, both of which predominantly deform via dislocation-mediated creep with correspondingly higher creep displacements and higher stress exponents.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under the specific conditions of room-temperature nanoindentation creep testing (5 mN load, variable loading rates, ~1 μm-thick coatings) deposited by RF magnetron sputtering. It has not been extended to macroscopic loading scenarios or elevated temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: While prior MD/HRTEM work and nanoindentation trends support the role of stress-induced amorphization at semicoherent interfaces, the exact contribution of this amorphous phase to creep resistance remains uncertain pending more direct in situ evidence.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayer coatings with modulation periods of 8, 16, 32, and 80 nm. Characterize the interfacial structure using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (including inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT)) to identify the nature (coherent, semicoherent, or grain boundary-dominated) and detect the presence of any amorphous phases. Subsequently, perform room-temperature nanoindentation creep testing under consistent conditions (5 mN load, chosen loading rates, 100 s dwell, and 20 s unloading) to measure creep displacement and strain rate. Analyze the data by plotting the natural logarithm of the creep strain rate against the logarithm of the flow stress to extract the creep stress exponent n.
measurements: XRD phase identification to confirm crystallographic state
TEM/IFFT imaging to determine interface coherency and presence of amorphous regions
Nanoindentation load–displacement curves to measure creep displacement
ln(strain rate) versus ln(flow stress) plots to extract creep stress exponent n
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the λ = 16 nm sample does not exhibit a significantly lower creep stress exponent (indicative of a shift to diffusion/interface-slip creep) along with evidence of stress-induced interfacial amorphization, and instead shows creep behavior similar to the λ = 8 nm or λ = 32/80 nm samples, then the hypothesis is rejected.
